questions.q: A satellite is in a steady circular orbit around the Earth. Which force acts as the centripetal force, and in what direction does it point?
options: An outward centrifugal force flinging the satellite away from the Earth
The gravitational attraction of the Earth, pointing inward toward the Earth's centre
The thrust of the satellite's engines, pointing along its direction of travel
A separate centripetal force added on top of gravity, pointing inward
questions.explanation: For a circular orbit the only real force acting is gravity, and it points inward toward the Earth's centre, which is the centre of the circle - so gravity IS the centripetal force. The centripetal force is never a new, extra force bolted on (option D): it is just the name for the net inward force. There is no engine or outward force in play.

questions.q: Setting the gravitational force equal to the centripetal force for a circular orbit gives v = √(GM/r). What does this tell you about the effect of the satellite's own mass on its orbital speed?
options: A heavier satellite must orbit faster to stay in the same orbit
A heavier satellite orbits more slowly at the same radius
The satellite's mass cancels, so orbital speed does not depend on it
The satellite's mass only matters for orbits close to the Earth
questions.explanation: When you write GMm/r² = mv²/r, the satellite mass m appears on both sides and cancels, leaving v = √(GM/r). Orbital speed depends only on the central mass M and the radius r, never on the satellite's mass - a tiny cubesat and a school-bus-sized craft in the same orbit move at exactly the same speed. Thinking a heavier satellite needs to go faster (option A) is a classic lost mark; if a question quotes the satellite's mass it is usually a distractor.

questions.q: The ISS orbits about 400 km up; a geostationary satellite orbits about 36 000 km up. Which is moving faster through space, and why?
options: The geostationary one, because it is higher and so has more energy and speed
The ISS, because a smaller orbital radius gives a larger speed (v = √(GM/r))
They move at the same speed, since orbital speed is independent of radius
The geostationary one, because it must keep pace with the Earth's spin
questions.explanation: Because v = √(GM/r) has the radius under a square root on the bottom, speed is inversely related to √r: the smaller-radius ISS moves faster (~7.7 km/s) while the far-out geostationary satellite crawls at ~3 km/s. Higher is slower but bigger-energy. Option A is the marquee trap of the topic - it confuses total energy (which does rise with height) with speed (which falls with height).

questions.q: A satellite orbits the Earth in a circular orbit at an altitude of 600 km. Calculate its orbital speed. Take M_E = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R_E = 6.37 × 10⁶ m, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
working: Altitude given, add the radius: \(r = R_E + h = 6.37 \times 10^{6} + 0.6 \times 10^{6} = 6.97 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}\)
questions.explanation: The three marks are for adding the altitude to the Earth's radius (r measured from the CENTRE), substituting into v = √(GM/r), and reaching about 7.6 × 10³ m/s. Forgetting to add the Earth's radius and using r = 600 km is the biggest error here.

questions.q: The International Space Station orbits at an altitude of about 400 km. Calculate its orbital speed. Take M_E = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, R_E = 6.37 × 10⁶ m, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
working: Radius from the Earth's centre: \(r = R_E + h = 6.37 \times 10^{6} + 0.4 \times 10^{6} = 6.77 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}\)
questions.explanation: The ISS radius is 6.77 × 10⁶ m and v = √(GM/r) gives ~7.67 × 10³ m/s, so it laps the Earth in about 92 minutes. Note this is faster than the 600 km satellite in the previous question - the lower orbit is quicker, exactly as 'higher is slower' predicts.

questions.q: A geostationary satellite has an orbital period of one day. Using Kepler's third law, calculate the radius of its orbit. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹, M_E = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, and one day = 86 400 s.
working: Rearrange Kepler's third law for \(r^3\): \(r^3 = \dfrac{G M T^2}{4\pi^2}\)
questions.explanation: The marks are for rearranging Kepler's third law to make r³ the subject, substituting the period in seconds, and taking the cube root to get about 4.22 × 10⁷ m. Subtracting the Earth's radius would give the altitude of about 35 800 km - the height every communications satellite sits at.

questions.q: Two moons orbit the same planet. The first has an orbital radius four times larger than the second. Determine how many times longer the first moon's orbital period is compared with the second's.
questions.given: \(r_1 = 4 r_2\),  same central mass, so Kepler's third law gives \(T^2 \propto r^3\)
working: Both moons orbit the same planet, so \(\dfrac{T^2}{r^3}\) is the same constant for both: \(T^2 \propto r^3\).
The radius grows by a factor of 4, so \(r^3\) grows by \(4^3 = 64\).
Therefore \(T^2\) grows by a factor of 64.
Take the square root: \(T\) grows by \(\sqrt{64} = 8\).
questions.explanation: The marks are for stating T² ∝ r³, cubing the factor of 4 to get 64, and then square-rooting to get a factor of 8. The trap is stopping at 64 and forgetting that the law relates period SQUARED to radius cubed - you must take the square root at the end.

questions.q: Kepler's second law states that a line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. What does this imply about a planet's speed around its orbit?
options: The planet moves at a constant speed everywhere around its orbit
The planet moves fastest when nearest the Sun and slowest when furthest away
The planet moves slowest when nearest the Sun and fastest when furthest away
The planet's speed depends only on its mass, not its distance from the Sun
questions.explanation: When the planet is close to the Sun the connecting line is short, so it must move quickly to sweep the same area; when far away the line is long, so it can sweep the same area while moving slowly. Hence planets move fastest at closest approach and slowest when furthest - this is really conservation of angular momentum. Option C reverses the relationship.

questions.q: Why must a geostationary satellite orbit directly above the equator, and not above a city such as Sydney?
options: Because the equator is the only place where gravity is strong enough to hold it
Because the plane of any orbit must pass through the Earth's centre, so only an equatorial orbit can stay fixed over one latitude all day
Because the Earth spins fastest at the equator, matching the satellite's speed
Because signals can only reach the ground from directly above the equator
questions.explanation: The centre of every orbit is the Earth's centre, so an orbit's plane must pass through that centre. The only circular orbit whose satellite can stay above a single fixed latitude is one lying in the equatorial plane. An orbit tilted to sit over Sydney would carry the satellite north and south of that latitude every few hours, so it could not stay fixed - it could be geosynchronous (24 h period) but would trace a figure-eight, not sit still.

questions.q: State Kepler's three laws of planetary motion, in order. What mnemonic helps you recall them?
keyPoints: First law (law of ellipses): each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun (central body) at one focus, not at the centre.
Second law (law of equal areas): a line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so the planet moves faster when nearer the Sun and slower when further away.
Third law (law of periods): the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the orbital radius, so T²/r³ is a constant for all bodies orbiting the same central mass.
Mnemonic: 'Every Astronomer Pauses' - Ellipse, Area, Period.
questions.explanation: One mark each in an exam. A weak answer that only gives the third (mathematical) law throws away two easy marks by forgetting the first two. If you named all three laws in order and recalled 'Every Astronomer Pauses', grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory, derive the orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit, and explain the two big consequences the episode draws from it.
keyPoints: For a circular orbit gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r.
Cancel the satellite mass m and one factor of r to get v² = GM/r, so v = √(GM/r).
Consequence 1: the satellite mass cancels, so orbital speed does not depend on the satellite's mass - only on the central mass M and radius r.
Consequence 2: r is under a square root on the bottom, so a larger radius means a smaller speed - 'higher is slower but bigger-energy' (speed falls with height, total energy rises).
Reminder: r is measured from the CENTRE of the central body, so 'altitude given, add the radius'.
questions.explanation: The derivation is the single most important move in the topic: equate gravity to centripetal force, cancel m and r, take the square root. If you produced v = √(GM/r) and stated both that mass cancels and that higher orbits are slower, grade yourself Good or Easy.
